content: 1. Request a demonstration that can be observed to understand the process better. 2. The top-down drug cost is calculated by multiplying the total annual quantity of drugs dispensed at the facility by the unit price of the drugs. 3. Top-down costing involves dividing the total expenditure on tuberculosis (TB) medication by the number of patients taking the medication. 4. This method typically uses step-down accounting techniques or allocation methods to break down aggregate costs into disaggregated costs for specific regimens or individual drugs. 5. For staff time allocation using a top-down measurement method, the ideal approach is to use staff timesheets for at least one cadre of healthcare workers performing each TB service output. 6. Based on the total time spent on each output, the proportion of time for each TB output is calculated in the Data Entry Tool. 7. If direct service personnel do not have timesheets, it is assumed that the proportion of time spent on TB is the same as other personnel in the same cadre. 8. For example, if timesheets are collected for one doctor, nurse, and nursing assistant, but additional doctors, nurses, and nursing assistants are providing TB services, the timesheet values for doctor 1 can be applied to doctor 2 and doctor 3 as well. 9. The same assumptions apply to other cadres. 10. For support staff, facility heads, or registrars, the proportion of time for TB is estimated based on the total TB outpatient visits divided by the total outpatient visits for the facility. 11. For heads of laboratory, radiology, and inpatient departments, use laboratory tests, radiology tests, and bed-days, respectively, to allocate time. 12. If direct measurement is not possible, service statistics can be used for allocation. 13. For healthcare workers providing outpatient services, estimate using the number of TB outpatient visits divided by the total outpatient visits. 14. For healthcare workers providing both outpatient and inpatient services, estimate using the number of TB outpatient visits plus TB inpatient bed-days divided by the total outpatient visits plus total inpatient bed-days. 15. For staff time allocation using a bottom-up measurement method, the ideal approach is to directly measure the number of hours and calculate the proportion of time spent on each task in the Data Entry Tool. 16. Alternatively, a rough estimate can be provided by staff interviews, or the percentage of time spent on TB can be calculated. 17. If a drug used at the facility is not included in the list, it should be added to the relevant section and the corresponding section in the 'Price list Drugs' sheet in the tool. 18. Bottom-up drug cost is calculated as the product of drug prices and the average quantity per average patient for each TB treatment and prevention regimen by phase. 19. For bottom-up costing, patient TB drug usage is analyzed. 20. In smaller facilities, this may involve abstracting all patients’ medication records, while in larger facilities, a sample of patient records might be used. 21. Care should be taken to ensure that transport costs are captured either in overhead costs, above-service-level costs, or vehicle costs (capital costs) and are not double-counted. 22. The life expectancy (in years) of each vehicle being costed must be provided. 23. If no locally specific value is available, include the value provided in the Parameters section. 24. The proportion of recurrent costs allocated to TB services is calculated using service statistics for outpatient visits (TB outpatient visits divided by total facility outpatient visits). 25. In cost analysis, overhead inputs are allocated to various departments or activities. 26. Inputs can be assigned to ‘cost centers’ depending on how cost data are organized and defined. 27. An allocation basis must be defined for allocating each input to various cost centers. 28. For example, some costs can be directly assigned to certain cost centers. 29. If ‘inpatient care’ is a cost center, the line item ‘laundry’ could be allocated to that center using ‘patient day equivalent’ as an allocation method. 30. If ‘maintenance’ is a cost center, ‘floor space utilized by department’ could be a useful allocation method. 31. Allocation of overhead inputs usually requires step-down costing. 32. The values in cells C13 to CE84 of the Service Description sheet should be copied and pasted into C14 to CE85 of the Data Entry Tool. 33. The transportation mark-up values for first-line and second-line drugs are linked to the formulae in column N. 34. The Service Description sheet in the data collection tool should be entered into the corresponding cell in the input sheet. 35. This sheet can be used to obtain drug prices from the facility or a central source such as the Ministry of Health or Regional Health Authority. 36. Ensure that the list of drugs is linked to the correct mark-up value based on the regimen they are used for. 37. Perform a spot check of the calculations of unit prices and costs per tablet/dose (local currency and USD) to ensure values from different rows are not being pulled in. 38. Drugs used to treat adverse events have not been included in the unit costs. 39. If this data is easily available and one wishes to include it, it can be entered in the ‘DRUGS: vaccines’ section. 40. Ensure that any edits or additions made to this sheet are replicated (with the same spelling and order) in the Drugs top-down and Drugs bottom-up sheets. 41. Vehicle, equipment, and furniture costs can be found in facility records and adjusted to the costed year or by contacting local medical and furniture suppliers for prices. 42. The bottom-up approach to costing these items involves auditing/counting how many there are within the facility. 43. The allocation of these costs to TB services is standardized within the sheets. 44. The top-down approach lists all equipment and furniture expenditures and allocates these to TB services using a standardized allocation factor specific to the different inputs. 45. The sheet multiplies the top-down unit costs of the service outputs by the quantity of each service output for an average patient for each population and regimen within each intervention type. 46. Patient costs are also provided by the phase of treatment and include the costs of drugs specific to the regimen and phase. 47. To check the results in this sheet, the analyst will perform a spot check to ensure the cells contain the correct values and that there are no missing or error values due to missing unit cost or quantity data. 48. Total costs for TB services are allocated for different input categories, and the allocation criteria for these categories are defined.
